title: Make a permanent alias in .bashrc or .zshrc
summary: An alias is a short name for a longer command. Writing it into your shell's startup file (.zshrc for zsh, .bashrc for bash) makes it work every time you open a terminal.

aliases.text: как добавить алиас в терминал мак

prerequisites: Know which shell you use: zsh is the default on macOS, bash is common on Linux

steps.explain: Check which shell you use. If the output ends with zsh, use ~/.zshrc. If it ends with bash, use ~/.bashrc.
steps.expect: /bin/zsh on a default macOS, or /bin/bash on many Linux systems.

steps.explain: Append the alias to the end of ~/.zshrc. The >> arrows add a line and keep the rest of the file.
steps.expect: No output. The file is created if it does not exist yet.

alternatives.explain: If you use bash, append the same line to ~/.bashrc instead.

steps.explain: Reload the file in the current terminal so the alias works right away. Opening a new terminal window also loads it.

alternatives.explain: Reload the bash file if you added the alias to ~/.bashrc.

verify.expect: bash: 'll is aliased to `ls -lah'' ; zsh: 'll is an alias for ls -lah'
A long list of the current folder, including hidden files whose names start with a dot.

rollback.explain: Open ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc in a text editor, delete the line that starts with alias ll=, save the file, then run source on that file again.

warnings: Use >> (two arrows), not > (one arrow). A single > replaces the whole file and deletes everything else in it.
Running the echo step twice adds the alias twice. This is harmless but messy; remove the extra line in the rollback step.
If ll already exists in the file, for example the default Ubuntu ~/.bashrc has alias ll='ls -alF', the line added at the end overrides it.
